newsitem.title: USA: Apple's stock extends rise on eve of trade show.
newsitem.headline: Apple's stock extends rise on eve of trade show.

text.p: Apple Computer Inc.'s stock extended its month-long climb Monday, fuelled by speculation that the growing involvement of co-founder Steve Jobs could help to turn the ailing company around.
Jobs, who is serving as a full-time adviser while Apple looks for a new chairman and chief executive, will deliver the keynote speech on Wednesday at the Macworld trade show in Boston.

Some industry watchers have speculated Jobs will announce the appointments of new, more computer-savvy members to the company's board of directors. Larry Ellison, the chairman of software company Oracle Corp., will be among them, according to French newspaper La Tribune, which published an interview with Ellison on Friday.
Ellison, a charismatic software billionaire, has long had an interest in buying Apple with his personal fortune.
"There's speculation that the management changes are going to increase the odds of Ellison buying the company," said Jim Poyner, analyst at investment bank Oppenheimer & Co. in New York.
The stock of Apple, based in Cupertino, Calif., rose 56 cents to hit $19.75 on Nasdaq -- up 50 percent from a month ago.

According to a story published in the New York Times on Friday, Jobs is pushing Apple to consider making cheaper Macintosh personal computers that draw their power from the Internet. Jobs and Ellison, who are personal friends, are big proponents of so-called network computers.
During the trade show, Apple is expected to preview several new, speedy Macs and to give out more details about the software, code-namded Rhapsody, for a new generation of Apple PCs in the works.
Whatever Jobs says, his growing influence at the company since the unexpected resignation of Chairman Gilbert Amelio last month has boosted morale among Apple employees and customers, analysts said.
"Steve is a good guy," said Barry Bosak, analyst at investment bank Smith Barney. "Steve returning to Apple is a good thing."

The long-running Apple soap opera escalated early last week when several newspapers reported that Jobs would once again become Apple chairman. Jobs, who founded the company in his early 20s from his parent's garage, was fired in 1985. He returned to the company as a part-time adviser in December when Apple, under then-chairman Amelio, bought Next Software Inc., the company Jobs founded after Apple.

But Jobs squelched talk that he would take the top job at Apple when he sent a memo last week to employees at Pixar Animations Studios, where he serves as chairman and chief executive officer, saying that he plans to remain at Pixar.
